chunks:
Rank any unadjusted county public-health dataset from highest to lowest and the top ten positions almost always share a familiar flaw: tiny rural counties dominate both extremes purely because small survey denominators amplify sampling noise. In public health epidemiology as much as in [civic data benchmarks](/explore/civic-data-benchmarks), mistaking small-sample binomial volatility for true clinical pathology misallocates emergency budgets and mobile clinic vans. Applying Empirical Bayes small-area shrinkage solves that distortion cleanly without hiding genuine geographic distress.

Federal modelers at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention already apply multilevel regression and poststratification when publishing county prevalence estimates. As the official CDC PLACES methodology documentation states:

> "PLACES uses small area estimation methods to produce census-tract, county, place, and ZCTA-level estimates of health-related outcomes and health risk behaviors based on Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System data and Census population demographics."

Once downloaded into [marigoldinsights](/explore/marigoldinsights) local or server pipelines, researchers can layer a second safeguard—Clayton-Kaldor Empirical Bayes shrinkage toward each state's prior distribution—across all 3,143 counties in the 2024 CDC PLACES GIS-friendly release. Weighting each county's age-adjusted prevalence by its inverse sampling variance shrinks noisy single-county spikes smoothly toward the state mean while leaving large urban hubs anchored to their empirical observations.

## Watching Empirical Bayes Shrinkage Work on Real Delta and Mountain Counties

Across all 3,143 matched counties nationwide, the 2024 CDC PLACES county average stands at 32.36% age-adjusted adult disability prevalence and 9.45% transportation insecurity. In rural counties with tiny populations, binomial variance is naturally wider, so Empirical Bayes pulls extreme estimates inward proportionately:

1. **Humphreys County, Mississippi (population 7,216):** Carries a raw age-adjusted disability rate of 46.30%, which Empirical Bayes adjusts modestly to 46.04% against Mississippi's statewide county average of 39.00%—confirming that Humphreys' burden is overwhelmingly structural rather than a tiny-sample artifact.
2. **Holmes County (population 15,777) and Tunica County (population 9,234):** Shift from raw rates of 45.30% and 45.20% to smoothed values of 45.20% and 45.02%, preserving their elevated priority rankings for mobile clinic outreach and ADA access support.
3. **Robeson County, North Carolina (population 117,365):** With a denominator fifteen times larger than Humphreys, Robeson retains nearly full credibility weight at 41.15% Empirical Bayes smoothed disability compared with 41.20% unadjusted, anchored above North Carolina's 33.35% 100-county mean.

## Answering the Fair Critique Against Statistical Shrinkage

Critics of hierarchical shrinkage caution that pulling extreme observations toward a statewide prior can mask real localized hazards—such as an isolated environmental cluster or abrupt mine closure inside a single rural township. That objection holds weight whenever between-county variance estimates dominate local anomalies or when true localized shocks drive sudden mortality spikes.

For that reason, reputable epidemiology workflows—built using reproducible [databases](/explore/databases) scripts in DuckDB and TypeScript—always preserve both columns side by side: unadjusted `disability_adj_prev` alongside `eb_smoothed_disability_pct`, plus raw `nchs_drug_mortality_rate` and explicit `hospital_desert_flag` indicators. Readers can verify where smoothing moves a borderline rural county and where severe underlying indicators—like Humphreys' 23.00% transportation barrier and 43.60% food insecurity—demand immediate physical intervention.

## Reading County Rankings Like an Epidemiologist on Tuesday Morning

Before citing any single-county morbidity anomaly, check three quantitative safeguards together: the adult population denominator behind the estimate, the CDC age-adjustment flag separating demographic retirement hubs from premature illness, and the distance between the raw prevalence and the Empirical Bayes posterior value. Look at how cleanly that discipline performs across our nationwide benchmark lake: in large suburban corridors, shrinkage changes almost nothing because survey precision is already tight; in remote rural counties with under 10,000 adults, Bayesian weighting tempers extreme single-cycle swings while leaving structural crisis spots like Humphreys County and Tunica County firmly anchored at the top.

Next time a legislative brief or dashboard screenshots a rural county at the top of a national morbidity chart, apply both raw rates and shrunk estimates side by side inside a reproducible browser workbook. When both raw prevalence and Clayton-Kaldor Empirical Bayes rates sit near the top—paired with corroborated [disaster continuity](/explore/disaster-continuity) storm exposure and scarce acute care—the epidemiological signal is genuine, durable, and ready for operational resource allocation. When a county disappears after Bayesian smoothing, you avoided chasing statistical fog.

---
**Sources:** [CDC PLACES 2024 County GIS CSV Release](https://data.cdc.gov/api/views/i46a-9kgh/rows.csv?accessType=DOWNLOAD) · [CDC PLACES Small-Area Methodology](https://www.cdc.gov/places/methodology/index.html) · [Clayton & Kaldor Empirical Bayes Estimator (PubMed 3676391)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3676391/)

County election administration lives downstream of physical geography, paved roads, and public transit—or the lack of it. While statutory debates focus on voter registration forms and postmark rules, public health micro-geography decides who can physically reach an in-person precinct on a Tuesday morning in November. Joining the 2024 CDC PLACES disability and transportation indicators directly against U.S. EAC 2024 EAVS V2.0 tables inside [election integrity](/explore/election-integrity) workbooks reveals stark operational gaps between neighboring states.

Federal accessibility law already mandates that election boards plan around mobility and cognitive barriers long before ballots print. As the U.S. Department of Justice ADA polling guidance reminds local officials:

> "Physical accessibility at polling places ensures that voters with mobility, vision, hearing, and cognitive disabilities can vote privately and independently in their local communities."

Across all 3,143 U.S. counties in the 2024 CDC PLACES release, adults report an average 32.36% age-adjusted prevalence of any disability and 9.45% lack of reliable transportation. When those federal public-health denominators join onto state audit files across Mississippi's 82 counties and North Carolina's 100 counties inside [marigoldinsights](/explore/marigoldinsights), two sharply different accessibility environments emerge.

## Comparing Mississippi's 82 Counties Against North Carolina's 100 Counties

Quantitative county averages demonstrate how health infrastructure and election logistics interlock:

1. **Mississippi Delta Mobility & Transit Deficit:** Across all 82 Mississippi counties, mean age-adjusted adult disability prevalence rises to 39.00%—nearly seven percentage points above the national county average—while lack of reliable transportation averages 14.28% and adult diabetes averages 14.76%. In rural Humphreys County, 46.30% of adults carry a disability, 25.40% report mobility limitations, 23.30% report cognitive limitations, and 23.00% lack reliable transportation. Neighboring Holmes County shows 45.30% disability and 22.50% transportation insecurity, while Tunica County records 45.20% disability and 22.10% transport barriers alongside 95 provisional ballots cast under strict in-person excuse requirements. 2.

**North Carolina High-Barrier Counties & Curbside Demands:** Across all 100 North Carolina counties, mean disability prevalence stands closer to national norms at 33.35% with 9.90% lacking transportation and 11.23% diabetes. Yet southern and northeastern counties face steep localized concentration: Robeson County records 41.20% disability, 20.70% mobility disability, 17.60% lacking transportation, and 1,167 provisional ballots cast in EAVS 2024; Scotland County registers 40.80% disability with 342 provisional ballots; and Halifax County logs 39.00% disability alongside 187 provisional ballots.

## Addressing the Causal-Attribution Objection

Public-health modelers and local clerks rightly note that county prevalence percentages from BRFSS behavioral surveys measure resident health risk across all adults rather than tracking which individual residents cast provisional or absentee ballots. High county disability prevalence cannot by itself prove that a specific ballot packet was rejected due to transit friction.

Instead, joining CDC PLACES with [civic data benchmarks](/explore/civic-data-benchmarks) identifies structural mismatch: when a county shows 20%+ mobility or transportation barriers alongside limited acute hospital care and strict excuse-only mail rules, precinct capacity and curbside poll-worker staffing must expand rather than contract.

## What Clerks and Civic Volunteers Should Measure Next

Local election boards can convert this cross-domain join into an immediate precinct checklist well ahead of candidate filing and early-voting site certification: overlay high-`civic_health_barrier_z` counties directly onto active polling-site ADA facility surveys, audit paved drop-off slopes, wheelchair ramp grades, and curbside call bells in every county above 40% adult disability prevalence, and stress-test [disaster continuity](/explore/disaster-continuity) shuttle routes for transit-isolated rural precincts where households lack daytime vehicles.

Because the underlying 3,143-county dataset joins deterministically on five-digit `county_fips` keys inside local browser compute, volunteer accessibility auditors and county clerks alike can inspect mobility barriers, cognitive disability prevalence, and provisional ballot counts side by side without ever uploading protected voter rosters to an external server. Pairing hard federal public-health denominators with transparent precinct logistics turns statutory equal-access guarantees into measurable field execution. Every citizen deserves equal ballot access regardless of zip code, age, mobility status, or car ownership.

---
**Sources:** [CDC PLACES 2024 County Release](https://data.cdc.gov/api/views/i46a-9kgh/rows.csv?accessType=DOWNLOAD) · [DOJ ADA Polling Place Checklist](https://www.ada.gov/resources/polling-places-checklist/) · [U.S. EAC 2024 EAVS V2.0 Public Data](https://www.eac.gov/sites/default/files/2026-02/2024_EAVS_for_Public_Release_nolabel_V2_csv.zip)

Emergency continuity models often measure storm damage solely in downed power lines and washed-out county roads, overlooking whether the county possesses a single acute-care hospital to stabilize displaced seniors or poll workers during an outage. Merging federal HHS hospital facility rosters with OpenFEMA disaster declarations and CDC NCHS mortality tables in [disaster continuity](/explore/disaster-continuity) models uncovers a brittle overlap across rural America.

Federal hospital data infrastructure tracks registered acute facilities primarily to coordinate surge readiness during public emergencies. As the HHS HealthData registry overview states:

> "The HHS registered hospital identification file catalogs acute care, critical access, and specialty facilities across U.S. states and territories to support national emergency capacity planning."

To honor strict [privacy](/explore/privacy) and zero-location-scraping discipline inside Marigold, ingestion scripts roll all 7,621 HHS facility rows strictly up to five-digit `county_fips` counts, discarding street addresses, coordinates, and facility strings immediately in memory. Out of 3,143 PLACES counties matched nationwide against 6,732 county-keyed hospitals, **659 U.S. counties—more than one in five—contain zero registered acute hospitals**.

## Where Hospital Deserts Collide with Disaster Declarations and Mortality Risk

Crossing `hospital_desert_flag == 1` with OpenFEMA declarations from 2020 through 2026 and the 3,136-county NCHS model-based drug poisoning dataset highlights distinct regional vulnerabilities: 1.

**Mississippi Delta Compound Fragility:** Eight of Mississippi's 82 counties qualify as acute hospital deserts, including top overall health-barrier outliers **Humphreys County** (0 hospitals, 11 FEMA declarations since 2020, 46.30% disability, 10.09 per 100k NCHS drug mortality rate) and **Tunica County** (0 hospitals, 7 FEMA declarations, 45.20% disability, and 18.91 per 100k NCHS mortality). Only one acute facility anchors Holmes County against 10 FEMA declarations and 53.10% adult hypertension. 2. **North Carolina's 18 Hospital Deserts & Mortality Peaks:** Eighteen of North Carolina's 100 counties lack an HHS-registered acute hospital inside county borders—requiring regional transport across mountain ridges or coastal floodplains when storms strike.

Even in counties served by a single hub, acute distress climbs steeply: Robeson County holds 1 hospital serving 117,365 residents alongside 8 FEMA declarations and a 43.03 per 100k NCHS drug mortality rate, while single-hospital Scotland County faces a 35.75 mortality rate.

## Evaluating the Cross-Border Commuting Counterargument

Healthcare geographers fairly note that county lines are political artifacts rather than strict clinical catchments: residents living five miles inside a "hospital desert" county frequently reach a Level-II trauma center across the county border faster than residents in a geographically sprawling single-hospital county. Treating `hhs_hospitals_count == 0` as zero healthcare access would overstate isolation near metro rings.

Yet combining county hospital counts with `lack_transport_adj_prev` (23.00% in Humphreys vs. 9.45% nationally) and [civic data benchmarks](/explore/civic-data-benchmarks) storm counts exposes where cross-county transit collapses. During major floods or Hurricane Helene corridor washouts, blocked highways turn neighboring county borders into hard medical walls.

## Turning Zstd Parquet Layers into Pre-Season Readiness Maps

County emergency managers, regional health coalitions, and rural transit authorities can inspect this exact cross-federal join inside [marigoldinsights](/explore/marigoldinsights) in one click using the 112.1 KB Zstd Parquet cube without provisioning cloud warehouses or proprietary GIS licenses. Filter nationwide rows where `hospital_desert_flag = 1` and `fema_disasters_2020_2026 >= 7`, rank counties by composite `civic_health_barrier_z`, and pair hospital scarcity against local nursing-home evacuation capacity and power-grid redundancy plans.

In practical field terms, identifying these 659 hospital-desert counties early lets mutual-aid coordinators pre-stage backup dialysis generators, oxygen-refill vans, and mobile EMS staging pads along higher-ground highway corridors months ahead of hurricane or flood season. When a severe storm isolates rural bridges across the Mississippi Delta or western North Carolina, pre-mapped hospital deserts prevent cascading emergency-room bottlenecks and protect medically fragile residents and volunteer poll workers alike before severe weather arrives.

---
**Sources:** [HealthData.gov HHS Registered Hospitals](https://healthdata.gov/api/views/vz64-k9wr/rows.csv?accessType=DOWNLOAD) · [CDC NCHS County Drug Mortality](https://data.cdc.gov/api/views/rpvx-m2md/rows.csv?accessType=DOWNLOAD) · [OpenFEMA DisasterDeclarationsSummaries v2](https://www.fema.gov/api/open/v2/DisasterDeclarationsSummaries)

Publishing public health metrics alongside civic administration files carries an obvious privacy hazard: the richer the cross-tabulation, the easier it becomes to re-identify an individual resident in a sparsely populated rural precinct. That danger explains why federal health agencies refuse to distribute unsuppressed individual tables—and why [privacy](/explore/privacy)-preserving analytics must enforce hard mathematical safeguards before any dataset leaves a server. Treating de-identification as a deterministic compiler pass rather than a policy memo keeps both clinical dignity and public auditability intact.

United States health privacy law codifies two explicit pathways—Safe Harbor removal of 18 identifier classes and formal statistical Expert Determination—before health statistics stop being regulated personal data. As HHS Office for Civil Rights guidance states:

> "In accordance with 45 CFR § 164.514(b), covered entities may de-identify protected health information by removing eighteen specific categories of identifiers, including names, street addresses, exact birth dates, and geographic subdivisions smaller than a state."

Although county boundaries represent larger jurisdictions than five-digit ZIP codes, CMS Medicare and NCHS mortality programs enforce an additional **small-cell suppression rule**: any tabulated numerator falling between 1 and 10 cases (`0 < n < 11`) must be suppressed rather than printed verbatim, preventing deduction by subtraction when row totals cross-tabulate with census denominators.

## How Marigold Enforces Zero-PII Across Server and Local Compute

Building trustworthy civic-health analytics inside [marigoldinsights](/explore/marigoldinsights) separates public statistical infrastructure from private individual files using three technical locks: 1. **Five-Digit FIPS Ceiling & Guardrails:** Server scripts aggregate CDC PLACES modeled percentages, 6,732 HHS hospital counts, and NCHS mortality estimates strictly to `county_fips` keys (`3,143` counties), stripping every facility street address, provider string, and coordinate before scanning 100% of serialized bytes through Marigold's `validateCivicContent` regex and secret guard. 2. **CMS `<11` Suppression & Laplace Noise Primitives:** Our server statistical refinery applies k-anonymity cell suppression (`minCellSize = 11`) to small-count outputs and supports parameterized Laplace($1/\epsilon$) differential privacy whenever local clinic partners export custom cross-tabulations. 3.

**Browser-Only Individual Joins:** If a municipal health board holds its own private clinic appointment log or local voter file in a [local-first](/explore/local-first) folder, those records never upload to any API route. Instead, the browser pulls the pre-compiled **112.1 KB Zstd Parquet shard** over HTTPS and executes the relational join inside local WebAssembly RAM using [databases](/explore/databases) DuckDB-Wasm workers.

## Addressing the Over-Suppression Objection

Quantitative researchers often frustrate over privacy rules because heavy cell suppression creates missing-data holes across Frontier and Great Plains counties—sometimes blocking trend lines where opioid or maternal mortality actually worsened. Excessive noise injection on small denominators can similarly invert regional rankings.

The clean engineering compromise is separating *model-based stabilized federal rates* (already smoothed hierarchically by NCHS and CDC) from *raw private numerators*: share the national county Parquet baselines openly via `/api/civic-lake`, suppress raw local counts below 11 cleanly, and keep exact individual audit calculations restricted to air-gapped local sessions.

## Building Privacy-Preserving Public Research Workflows

Before merging any external health file into a civic brief or publishing a county-level scoreboard, engineering teams should enforce four concrete privacy invariants in automated continuous integration rather than relying on manual spreadsheet review: verify zero personal identifiers, street coordinates, or sub-county keys exist above five-digit `county_fips`; apply deterministic CMS `< 11` small-cell suppression on any derived event count numerator; run automated pattern-matching scanners for SSNs, names, dates of birth, and raw facility locations before committing static artifacts; and confirm SHA-256 content hashes between CSV and Zstd Parquet compilations.

By separating public federal county benchmarks cleanly from private local workflows, civic analysts gain full statistical depth while keeping individual neighbors protected. Strong civic transparency and rigorous open-source auditing never require exposing a single person's medical history or residential record to a third-party server.

---
**Sources:** [HHS OCR HIPAA De-Identification Guidance (45 CFR § 164.514)](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/special-topics/de-identification/index.html) · [CMS ResDAC Cell Size Suppression Policy](https://resdac.org/articles/cms-cell-size-suppression-policy) · [CDC PLACES 2024 GIS County CSV](https://data.cdc.gov/api/views/i46a-9kgh/rows.csv?accessType=DOWNLOAD)
